task_description: I need to email managers about a new policy requiring them to document performance concerns before initiating any PIP — we've had inconsistency and some legal exposure.

rubric_used.user_goals_summary: Writes HR communications that treat employees as intelligent adults who deserve to understand why things change. Prioritizes trust-building through transparency and precision over polished corporate messaging.

rubric.name: Problem-First Policy Framing
rubric.description: Policy changes lead with the employee-facing problem the policy solves, not with the policy itself. The reader should understand and care about the 'why' before encountering the 'what.'

dimensions.label: The email describes the problem or need before introducing the policy change
The problem is framed from the employee's experience, not the company's operational needs
The rationale appears before the specific details of the change

rubric.name: Decision Attribution
rubric.description: Decisions are attributed to 'we' or 'the team,' never 'I decided.' The sender avoids making themselves the target by using collective framing, which channels responses toward constructive feedback rather than personal pushback.

dimensions.label: Decisions use 'we' or 'the leadership team' as subject, not 'I'
Does not frame the change as the sender's personal choice or preference
Questions are directed toward understanding, not appealing the decision — 'questions about how this works' not 'if you disagree'

rubric.name: Named Human Contact Point
rubric.description: Questions are directed to a specific named person, not a role or generic channel. 'Ask Jamal in Benefits' not 'Contact HR.' Naming the person signals accessibility and accountability.

dimensions.label: The point of contact is a specific person's name, not a department or role title
Includes how to reach them (Slack, email, office hours) — not just 'reach out'
Does not use 'contact HR' or 'reach out to your manager' without a name

rubric.name: Absolute Date Precision
rubric.description: Any change affecting compensation, benefits, or workload includes exact dates — never relative timeframes like 'in the coming weeks' or 'soon.' People planning their lives need precision.

dimensions.label: All timelines use specific dates (e.g., 'March 15') not relative terms ('next month', 'soon')
The effective date of the change is stated explicitly, not implied
If there's a transition period, both start and end dates are provided

rubric_used.coaching_notes: Miriam's non-negotiable is that employees are treated as adults who deserve the full picture. Will reject any draft that buries the 'why' or uses vague timelines. Prefers warmth but will sacrifice it for precision — never the reverse.

rounds.draft:
Subject: New Step Before Starting a PIP — What's Changing and Why

Hi everyone,

We want to share a change to how we handle performance improvement plans, and we'd like to start with what prompted it.

Over the past year, we've seen real inconsistency in how PIPs get initiated across teams. In some cases, employees have entered a formal PIP without any prior documented conversation about the concern — which isn't fair to them, and has created legal exposure for the company when those situations are later reviewed. People deserve to know a concern exists before it becomes a formal process. And when documentation is sparse, it's hard for anyone — the employee, their manager, or HR — to understand the full picture.

**What's changing**

Starting **February 3, 2025**, initiating a PIP will require at least one prior documented performance conversation on record. That documentation should capture the specific concern, the date of the conversation, and what was discussed in terms of expectations going forward. It doesn't need to be lengthy — a few clear sentences in the employee's file is sufficient.

This isn't a new bureaucratic hurdle. It's a floor we should already have been meeting, and formalizing it gives everyone — including you — a clearer record to stand on.

**What this means for you**

If you're currently managing a performance concern and anticipate a PIP may be needed, please make sure at least one documented conversation is on file before February 3. If you're unsure whether your existing notes meet the standard, that's worth checking now rather than later.

Going forward, HR will confirm documentation is in place before countersigning any PIP.

**Questions?**

Reach out to **Priya Anand** directly — she's the right person to talk through specific situations or edge cases. You can message her on Slack at **@priya.anand** or email her at **priya.anand@[company].com**. She's also holding open office hours on **January 22 and January 29** (10–11 a.m.) for anyone who wants to talk it through in real time.

We know this adds a step, and we appreciate you working with us to get it right. The goal is a process that's fair to employees and gives managers a solid foundation when difficult conversations are necessary.

Thanks,
[Your name]

The problem is framed from the employee's experience ('People deserve to know a concern exists before it becomes a formal process'), not purely from operational or legal needs — though legal exposure is mentioned as a secondary point, it doesn't lead. All three dimensions are clearly satisfied.

The contact is a specific named person (Priya Anand), with two explicit channels (Slack @priya.anand and email address), and scheduled office hours with exact dates and times (January 22 and January 29, 10–11 a.m.). There is no generic 'contact HR' language anywhere. All three dimensions are unambiguously satisfied.

hidden_pref_satisfaction.evidence: The second paragraph opens with the problem: 'employees have entered a formal PIP without any prior documented conversation about the concern — which isn't fair to them' — framing the issue from the employee's perspective before introducing the policy change.

hidden_pref_satisfaction.preference: Use 'you/your' heavily but never 'I' in subject position; decisions come from 'we' or 'the team'
hidden_pref_satisfaction.evidence: The draft uses 'we' throughout ('We want to share,' 'we've seen,' 'we appreciate') and 'you/your' extensively ('What this means for you,' 'If you're currently managing'). No instance of 'I' appears in the subject position.

hidden_pref_satisfaction.preference: Name a specific PERSON as the contact, not a role or generic 'reach out'
hidden_pref_satisfaction.evidence: 'Reach out to Priya Anand directly — she's the right person to talk through specific situations or edge cases. You can message her on Slack at @priya.anand or email her at priya.anand@[company].com.'
